name: STM32G474RBT3
title: STM32G474xB/xC/xE Arm Cortex-M4 microcontrollers with FPU, 170 MHz, 128 to 512 Kbytes Flash, 128 Kbytes SRAM, math accelerators, rich analog and a 184 ps high-resolution timer, 1.71 V to 3.6 V
summary: A Cortex-M4F microcontroller line running at up to 170 MHz (213 DMIPS) from a 1.71 V to 3.6 V supply, with 128, 256 or 512 Kbytes of dual-bank ECC Flash, 128 Kbytes of SRAM and CORDIC and FMAC math engines. Its analog side has five 12-bit ADCs, seven DAC channels, seven comparators, six op-amps and a reference buffer; its timers include a high-resolution timer with 12 outputs at 184 ps resolution and three motor-control timers; it carries three FDCANs, a full-speed USB device, a USB Type-C Power Delivery controller, an FSMC and a Quad-SPI interface, in packages of 48 to 128 pins. STM32G474RBT3 is the 128 Kbyte LQFP64 part for -40 °C to 125 °C ambient, with 52 GPIOs.
key_figures: Arm Cortex-M4 with FPU, MPU and DSP instructions, up to 170 MHz, 213 DMIPS
128, 256 or 512 Kbytes Flash (ECC, two banks), 128 Kbytes SRAM (80 + 16 + 32 CCM)
VDD 1.71 V to 3.6 V; VDDA 1.62 V to 3.6 V; VBAT 1.55 V to 3.6 V
six 16-bit counters plus master, 12 outputs, 184 ps resolution
five 12-bit ADCs, 0.25 µs, up to 42 channels, 16 bits by oversampling, 0 V to 3.6 V input
seven 12-bit channels: three buffered external at 1 Msps, four internal unbuffered at 15 Msps
seven comparators, six op-amps with PGA, VREFBUF at 2.048 V, 2.5 V or 2.9 V
3 FDCAN, 4 I2C, 3 USART, 2 UART, LPUART, 4 SPI (2 with I2S), SAI, USB FS device, UCPD
4 to 48 MHz crystal, 32 kHz crystal, HSI16 ±1%, LSI 32 kHz ±5%, HSI48
-40 °C to 85 °C or -40 °C to 125 °C ambient by order code

(1) Which functions exist depends on the device chosen.

(2) PC13, PC14 and PC15 draw their supply through the power switch, which sinks no more than 3 mA. Used as outputs they are limited to 2 MHz into at most 30 pF, and they must not source current (an LED, for example).
(3) Once the backup domain has powered up, PC13, PC14 and PC15 act as GPIOs governed by the RTC registers, which a system reset does not clear (reference manual RM0440).
(4) Out of reset these pins carry the JTAG/SW debug functions, with the internal pull-up switched on at PA15, PA13 and PB4 and the internal pull-down at PA14.

(5) From reset, the UCPD can switch a 5.1 kΩ pull-down (Rd) onto PB6 (UCPD1_CC1) and PB4 (UCPD1_CC2): a high level on PA9 (UCPD1_DBCC1) turns on the one at PB6, and a high level on PA10 (UCPD1_DBCC2) the one at PB4. This dead-battery pull-down is removed by setting UCPD1_DBDIS = 1 in PWR_CR3.
(6) If PB8 is left unconnected, putting it in a mode other than analog after start-up keeps its consumption down.
In UFQFPN48 the VSS connections are made through the exposed pad.

circuits.description: Supply pins and their decoupling. A 1.55 V to 3.6 V backup source feeds VBAT. The VDD pins share one 100 nF ceramic capacitor per pin plus one 4.7 µF capacitor to VSS. VDDA has 10 nF plus 1 µF to VSSA, and VREF+ has 100 nF plus 1 µF to VSSA. Each capacitor sits as close to its pins as possible, or under them on the far side of the board.

circuits.title: Recommended NRST pin protection
circuits.description: A 0.1 µF capacitor from NRST to ground, placed close to the part, guards against parasitic resets; a push button to ground is the external reset. NRST has its own pull-up RPU to VDD inside, followed by a Schmitt trigger and a filter. The external circuit must be able to pull NRST below VIL(NRST) max or the reset is ignored.

operation.text: Three Flash sizes (xB 128 Kbytes, xC 256 Kbytes, xE 512 Kbytes) in nine packages of 48 to 128 pins. Two temperature ranges: -40 °C to +85 °C ambient (+105 °C junction) and -40 °C to +125 °C ambient (+130 °C junction). Peripherals sit on two APB and two AHB buses joined by a 32-bit multi-AHB matrix. Flash and SRAM can be guarded by readout protection, write protection, PCROP (an execute-only code area) and a securable area. The FSMC is on the devices of 100 pins and more.

Arm Cortex-M4 32-bit RISC core at up to 170 MHz (213 DMIPS) with a single-precision FPU covering all Arm single-precision instructions and data types, the full DSP instruction set and a memory protection unit.
A memory accelerator in front of the Flash hides its wait states from the Cortex-M4, giving zero-wait-state execution from Flash at up to 170 MHz.

The MPU splits memory into as many as 8 regions, each divisible into 8 subregions, with region sizes from 32 bytes up to the full 4 Gbyte space. An access the MPU forbids lets an RTOS catch a task that strays; applications that do not need it can leave it bypassed.

Up to 512 Kbytes for code and data, run as one bank or two; in dual-bank mode one bank can be read while the other is erased or programmed, and boot from either bank is supported. Option bytes set readout protection Level 0 (none), Level 1 (Flash closed when debug is attached or when booting from RAM or the bootloader) or Level 2 (debug, RAM boot and bootloader disabled for good, irreversible); write protection of chosen areas; PCROP, an execute-only area reachable only by CPU instruction fetches, with option bit PCROP_RDP deciding whether it is wiped when RDP goes from Level 1 back to Level 0; and a securable area that behaves as normal Flash after reset until it is locked, after which every access to it faults until the next reset, so boot code and keys can run once and then be hidden. ECC corrects single-bit and detects double-bit errors, and the failing address is held in a register. A 1 Kbyte OTP area (128 double words) in Bank 1 can be written once and never erased.

128 Kbytes in three blocks, all readable and writable at full CPU speed with no wait states. SRAM1: 80 Kbytes at 0x2000 0000 on the system bus (or on I-Code/D-Code when booting from SRAM1 or remapped through SYSCFG_MEMRMP), parity-checked over its first 32 Kbytes. SRAM2: 16 Kbytes at 0x2001 4000 on the system bus, retainable in Standby. CCM SRAM: 32 Kbytes at 0x1000 0000 on the I-Code/D-Code bus for the fastest CPU access, also aliased at 0x2001 8000 so the CPU and both DMAs see it right after SRAM1 and SRAM2; parity-checked and write-protectable in 1 Kbyte steps.

A 32-bit multi-AHB matrix lets the CPU (I-bus, D-bus, S-bus) and the two DMA controllers reach the Flash through the accelerator, SRAM1, SRAM2, CCM SRAM, the AHB1 and AHB2 peripherals, the FSMC and the QUADSPI concurrently.

BOOT0 (from pin PB8-BOOT0, or from option bit nBOOT0 when option bit nBOOT_SEL frees the pin) together with option bit nBOOT1 picks user Flash, system memory or embedded SRAM at start-up. The bootloader in system memory reprograms the Flash over USART, I2C, SPI or USB DFU.

Hardware engine for trigonometric and related functions: a 24-bit CORDIC rotation core in circular or hyperbolic mode, rotation or vectoring, computing cos, sin, cosh, sinh, atan2, atan, atanh, square root, modulus and natural log. Precision is programmable up to 20 bits and it converges at 4 bits per clock. Inputs and outputs are 16-bit or 32-bit fixed point over a low-latency AHB slave port; a result may be read the moment it exists, without polling or an interrupt, and DMA can feed and drain it.

Filter accelerator built around a 16 × 16-bit multiplier and a 24+2-bit accumulator that adds or subtracts, on 16-bit data held in a 256 × 16-bit local memory. Up to three buffers (two input, one output) are placed by base-pointer and size registers and may be circular, with a watermark to cut interrupt load. It runs FIR and direct-form-1 IIR filters, has an AHB slave port and DMA read and write channels.

Computes a CRC with a configurable generator polynomial and size, for checking transmitted or stored data; under EN/IEC 60335-1 it serves to verify the Flash contents against a signature made at link time.

VDD, 1.71 V to 3.6 V, feeds the I/O ring, the core regulator, and the reset, power-management and internal-clock circuits. VDDA, 1.62 V to 3.6 V, powers the ADCs, DACs, VREFBUF, op-amps and comparators independently of VDD and is best tied to VDD when those blocks are unused; each analog block's own minimum VDDA is set in the electrical characteristics. VBAT, 1.55 V to 3.6 V, keeps the RTC, the 32 kHz oscillator and the backup registers alive through a power switch while VDD is absent. VREF+ is the reference of the ADCs and DACs and the output of the reference buffer when it is on (2.048 V, 2.5 V or 2.9 V, chosen by the VRS bits of VREFBUF_CSR; the third level is misprinted 2.95 V in the supply description and should read 2.9 V): with VDDA below 2 V it must equal VDDA; with VDDA at 2 V or more it may be anywhere from 2 V to VDDA. VREF- is bonded to VSSA.

A brown-out reset, active in every mode except Shutdown, holds the part in reset while VDD is under its threshold, so no external reset circuit is needed. Its lowest level is 1.71 V at power-on; higher levels are chosen in the option bytes. A programmable voltage detector, enabled by software, compares VDD with VPVD and can interrupt when VDD falls below or rises above it. A peripheral voltage monitor checks VDDA against a fixed level so the analog blocks run only inside their supply range.

A main regulator (MR) serves Run and Sleep; a low-power regulator (LPR) serves Stop and the two low-power run and sleep modes. Both shut down, outputs high-impedance, in Standby and Shutdown. The core voltage follows dynamic voltage scaling: Range 1 boost mode allows a CPU clock up to 170 MHz, Range 1 normal mode up to 150 MHz, and Range 2 up to 26 MHz.

Run follows any reset. Sleep stops only the CPU; any peripheral interrupt or event wakes it. Low-power run feeds the core from the low-power regulator, limits the CPU to 2 MHz from Flash or SRAM, and lets peripherals with their own clock run on HSI16. Low-power sleep is entered from Low-power run, stops the CPU clock, and returns to Low-power run on wakeup. Stop keeps SRAM and registers but halts every clock of the core domain, with PLL, HSI16 and HSE off and LSE or LSI still running; the RTC may stay on, and peripherals able to wake the part may switch HSI16 on to handle the event. Standby turns the regulator off and loses SRAM and registers except the RTC domain and standby circuitry, keeps the BOR running, lets software choose a pull-up, pull-down or nothing for each I/O, and wakes on NRST, an IWDG reset, a WKUP pin edge (rising or falling), an LSE failure, or an RTC alarm, wakeup, timestamp or tamper event. Shutdown also stops LSI, has no BOR and no supply monitoring (so no switch to the RTC domain), keeps only the RTC-domain registers, and wakes on NRST, an IWDG reset, a WKUP pin edge or an RTC alarm, wakeup, timestamp or tamper event.
During and after reset the I/Os sit in analog state with their Schmitt triggers off, to cut consumption, and the internal pull-up on the reset pin is switched off when the reset comes from inside.

VBAT can come from a battery, a supercapacitor, or VDD when no battery is fitted and a supercapacitor is. It feeds the RTC with the LSE and the backup registers, and three anti-tamper pins work in VBAT mode. The switch to VBAT happens by itself when VDD disappears. An internal charger can charge a battery on VBAT while VDD is present. External interrupts and RTC alarms or events do not bring the part out of VBAT operation.

Direct links between peripherals let them trigger one another without the CPU, at low and fixed latency; which links work in Run, Sleep, the low-power run and sleep modes and Stop is given in the interconnect matrix.

SYSCLK comes from the HSE (4 to 48 MHz crystal or ceramic resonator, or an external clock in bypass), the HSI16 (16 MHz RC, software-trimmable, ±1%) or the PLL (fed by HSE or HSI16, up to 170 MHz). The internal 48 MHz RC (HSI48) with clock recovery can clock the USB or the RNG. The RTC runs from the LSE (32.768 kHz crystal with four drive levels, or bypass) or the LSI (32 kHz RC, ±5%, which also clocks the IWDG). I2S, USART, I2C, LPTIM, ADC, SAI and RNG can take a clock independent of the system clock. Prescalers set the AHB, APB2 (high speed) and APB1 (low speed) clocks, all up to 170 MHz, and the controller gates clocks to the core, peripherals and memory and switches sources safely on the fly. The clock security system moves SYSCLK to HSI16 and can interrupt if the HSE fails; an LSE failure can also be flagged. MCO puts an internal clock on a pin; LSCO puts LSI or LSE on a pin in every low-power mode.

Each GPIO is set by software as an output (push-pull or open-drain), an input (floating, pulled up or pulled down) or an alternate function of a peripheral; most share digital or analog functions. They sit on AHB2 for fast toggling, and a locking sequence can freeze their configuration.

Two controllers with 8 channels each, 16 in all, every channel tied to a hardware request and also software-triggerable. Priority is set by software in four levels (very high, high, medium, low) and, at equal level, by channel number. Source and destination sizes (byte, half word, word) are independent, with packing and unpacking; addresses must align to the data size. Circular buffers are supported, and transfers may go between any pair of memory and peripheral (memory to memory included); Flash, SRAM and the APB and AHB peripherals can each be either end, with up to 65536 data per transfer. Half-transfer, transfer-complete and transfer-error flags combine into one interrupt per channel.

DMAMUX routes the request lines of the peripherals to the DMA channels; each channel picks one request, either directly or synchronised to events on its synchronisation inputs. A built-in request generator makes DMA requests from trigger inputs.
The 16 Cortex-M4 interrupt lines and up to 102 maskable channels, at 16 priority levels, with low-latency entry, late-arrival and tail-chaining handling and automatic state saving.

44 edge-detector lines raise interrupts or events and wake the part from Stop; each takes a rising, falling or both-edge trigger and can be masked on its own. Pulses narrower than one internal clock period are still caught. The 16 external lines take up to 107 GPIOs between them; internal lines come from peripherals that can wake from Stop.

Five successive-approximation ADCs, 12 bits native with built-in calibration, 4 Msps at full resolution with a sampling time down to 41.67 ns, faster at lower resolution (6.66 Msps at 6 bits). Inputs are single-ended or differential. An external reference pin exists on every package. Current falls in proportion to conversion rate, and the ADC clock is independent of the CPU clock. Two groups (regular and injected) run single, continuous or discontinuous scans started by software, timers or external signals; results go to a data register or to RAM by DMA, with left or right alignment, per-channel offset, hardware gain and offset correction, per-channel sampling time, an analog watchdog that can interrupt or trigger timers, context preparation for injected channels, and an oversampling unit for better SNR.

A sensor whose output VTS rises linearly with temperature feeds internal ADC channels. Its offset varies from part to part, so without calibration it only tracks changes; each part carries factory readings at 30 °C (TS_CAL1) and 110 °C (TS_CAL2), taken at VDDA = VREF+ = 3.0 V, in read-only system memory.

VREFINT is a bandgap voltage for the ADCs and comparators, on channel ADCx_IN18 for x = 1, 3, 4, 5. Its exact value, measured for each part at 30 °C and VDDA = VREF+ = 3.0 V, is stored in read-only system memory.
Internal channel ADC1_IN17 reads VBAT through a divide-by-3 bridge, so the converted value is one third of VBAT and stays within the ADC range when VBAT is above VDDA.
Each op-amp output OPAMPxINT (x = 1 to 6) can be sampled on an internal channel of the ADCs (x = 1 to 5), leaving the I/O that would carry the output free as a GPIO.

Seven 12-bit channels: three buffered external channels at up to 1 Msps and four unbuffered internal channels at up to 15 Msps. Each is a resistor string followed by an inverting amplifier. Features: up to two outputs per DAC, 8-bit or 12-bit mode, factory and user offset trimming of the buffer, left or right alignment in 12-bit mode, synchronised update, noise, triangle and sawtooth generation, independent or simultaneous dual conversion, DMA per channel, external triggers (timer update outputs among them), and a low-power sample-and-hold mode with an internal or external capacitor.

An internal buffer drives VREF+ as the reference for the ADCs and DACs and for parts outside the chip, at 2.048 V, 2.5 V or 2.9 V. With the buffer off, an outside reference can be applied on VREF+. In packages where VREF+ is bonded together with VDDA the buffer cannot be used. The VREF+ pin takes a 100 nF capacitor that sets the low-frequency cut-off of the buffer output.

Seven comparators, rail to rail, whose hysteresis can be programmed. The reference input can be an I/O, a DAC output, VREFINT or 1/4, 1/2 or 3/4 of it. Every comparator can wake the part from Stop, interrupt, and drive timer breaks.

Six op-amps with 13 MHz bandwidth and rail-to-rail input and output, routable as followers inside or outside the chip, and usable as PGAs with non-inverting gains of 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 or 64 or inverting gains of -1, -3, -7, -15, -31 or -63; all terminals reach pins.
A true random number generator built on an analog noise source delivers 32-bit values.

HRTIM is seven timers, one master and six slaves, with 12 high-resolution outputs that pair up for dead-time insertion, 6 fault inputs for protection and 10 external-event inputs for signals such as current limit or zero-voltage and zero-current detection. A digital core clocked at 170 MHz is followed by delay lines held in closed loop, giving 184 ps resolution independent of voltage, temperature and process spread, on all 12 outputs whichever is varied: duty cycle, frequency, or neither with a fixed on-time. Slave timers can be combined to drive multi-switch converters or run separate converters. Waveforms are built from programmed timings and outside events such as analog or digital feedback, with blanking and filtering of spurious events and faults, DMA requests, a burst-mode controller, and push-pull and resonant modes. Topologies named: LLC, phase-shifted full bridge, buck or boost in voltage or current mode, and fluorescent or LED lighting; it also serves as a general-purpose timer, for example as a fine-grained DAC made from PWM. When debugging, the counters freeze and the outputs go to their safe state.

TIM1, TIM8 and TIM20 each give four channels with complementary outputs and programmable dead time, eight PWM outputs in all. Channels do input capture, output compare, edge- or center-aligned PWM over 0 to 100% and one-pulse output. In debug the counter can be frozen and the outputs disabled to turn off power switches. They share architecture with the general-purpose timers and can be linked to them for synchronisation or chaining.

TIM2 and TIM5 have 32-bit auto-reload up/down counters and 32-bit prescalers; TIM3 and TIM4 are the 16-bit versions. All four have four channels for capture, compare, PWM or one-pulse, quadrature-encoder inputs and their own DMA requests. TIM15 (two channels, one complementary), TIM16 and TIM17 (one channel, one complementary each) have 16-bit up counters and prescalers. All can be linked for synchronisation and frozen in debug.
TIM6 and TIM7 are 16-bit time bases, chiefly for triggering the DACs.

LPTIM1 has its own clock and keeps counting in Stop when its clock is LSE, LSI or an outside source, from which it can wake the part. It has a 16-bit up counter with 16-bit autoreload and compare, pulse or PWM output, continuous or one-shot runs, software or hardware triggers, a digital glitch filter and an encoder mode. Clock sources: LSE, LSI, HSI16 or the APB clock, or an external clock on its input that counts pulses even with no internal clock running.

12-bit down counter with an 8-bit prescaler, clocked by the 32 kHz LSI so it runs on in Stop and Standby. It resets the part on a fault or serves as a free-running timeout timer; option bytes select hardware or software start, and it can be frozen in debug.
7-bit down counter clocked from the main clock, able to free-run, with an early-warning interrupt; it resets the part on a fault and can be frozen in debug.
24-bit down counter with autoreload, a programmable clock source and a maskable interrupt at zero, meant for an RTOS tick or general counting.

BCD calendar with subseconds, seconds, minutes, hours (12 or 24 h), weekday, date, month and year, correcting itself for 28, 29, 30 and 31-day months. Two alarms; shift correction of 1 to 32767 RTC clock pulses for syncing to a master clock; reference-clock input (50 or 60 Hz) for better accuracy; digital calibration in 0.95 ppm steps; timestamp on a pin event, a tamper event or a switch to VBAT; and a 17-bit auto-reload wakeup timer. It is supplied from VDD, or from VBAT when VDD is absent. Clock sources: 32.768 kHz LSE crystal, an outside resonator or oscillator on LSE, the LSI (about 32 kHz), or HSE divided by 32. On LSE it works in VBAT mode and all low-power modes; on LSI it works in every low-power mode except Shutdown and not in VBAT mode. Alarm, wakeup timer and timestamp events can interrupt and wake the part from low-power modes.

32 backup registers of 32 bits are kept in every low-power mode and in VBAT mode and are not cleared by system or power reset or by waking from Standby or Shutdown. Up to three tamper pins detect edges, edge and level, or filtered level; five internal tamper sources exist as well. Any tamper event erases the backup registers, can timestamp the RTC, and can interrupt and wake the part from every low-power mode.

IRTIM combines TIM17 channel 1 (carrier) and TIM16 channel 1 (data) internally into IR_OUT, available on PB9 or PA13; programming the two output-compare channels yields the standard IR modulation schemes.

Four I2C interfaces following I2C-bus specification rev. 5: master and slave, multimaster, Standard-mode up to 100 kbit/s, Fast-mode up to 400 kbit/s and Fast-mode Plus up to 1 Mbit/s with 20 mA drive I/Os, 7- and 10-bit addressing (with more than one 7-bit own address), programmable setup and hold timing, and clock stretching that can be turned off. SMBus 2.0 with hardware PEC, ARP and alert; PMBus 1.1. Each has an independent clock source so the bus rate does not follow PCLK changes, wakes from Stop on address match, has programmable analog and digital noise filters, and a 1-byte buffer served by DMA.

USART1, USART2 and USART3 are synchronous/asynchronous; UART4 and UART5 are asynchronous only. All do IrDA SIR, multiprocessor mode, single-wire half duplex, LIN master/slave, CTS/RTS flow control and RS485 driver enable; the three USARTs add ISO 7816 smartcard and SPI-like synchronous mode. Each has 8-entry transmit and receive FIFOs, off by default, a clock domain separate from the CPU, wakeup from Stop on start bit, any frame, a chosen frame or FIFO status, and DMA service.

One low-power UART for asynchronous links with half-duplex single wire, CTS/RTS and multiprocessor mode, transmit and receive FIFOs (off by default), its own clock domain and DMA service. It wakes the part from Stop on start bit, any frame, a chosen frame or FIFO status. Running from the 32.768 kHz LSE alone it reaches 9600 baud, so it can wait for a frame in Stop on very little energy; a faster clock gives higher baud rates.

Four SPIs reach 75 Mbit/s as master and 41 Mbit/s as slave in full duplex, half duplex or simplex, with frames of 4 to 16 bits, eight master rates from a 3-bit prescaler, hardware CRC, TI mode and NSS pulse mode. SPI2 and SPI3 double as half-duplex I2S master or slave in four audio standards, transferring 16, 24 or 32 bits at 16- or 32-bit resolution, at sampling rates from 8 kHz to 192 kHz set by an 8-bit linear prescaler, and as master can output a 256 × fs clock for an audio codec. All are served by DMA.

One serial audio interface with two sub-blocks, each a transmitter or receiver with its own 8-word FIFO, synchronous or not, master or slave, each with its own clock generator. Protocols include I2S, PCM/DSP, TDM, AC’97, LSB- or MSB-justified formats, and SPDIF output; data of 8, 10, 16, 20, 24 or 32 bits; up to 16 slots with selectable active slots; configurable frame length, frame sync level, offset and width, first-bit position, bit order and clock edge; mute and stereo or mono. It flags overrun, underrun, early or late frame sync in slave mode and AC’97 codec-not-ready, and has two DMA channels, one per sub-block.

Three CAN controllers (FDCAN1, FDCAN2, FDCAN3) meeting ISO 11898-1 (CAN 2.0 A and B) and CAN FD 1.0 share a 3 Kbyte message RAM that holds their filters, receive FIFOs and buffers, transmit event FIFOs and transmit buffers.

Full-speed (12 Mbit/s) USB 2.0 device with an internal PHY, embedded DP pull-up, Battery Charging 1.2 detection, Link Power Management, suspend and resume, and up to 1 Kbyte of packet memory for its configurable endpoints. It needs an exact 48 MHz clock: from the PLL running on an HSE crystal, or from the internal 48 MHz oscillator trimmed automatically from the USB SOF stream, which allows operation with no crystal.

One USB Type-C and Power Delivery controller (Type-C rev. 1.2, PD rev. 3.0) on dedicated I/Os that carry the Rp pull-ups (all values) and Rd pull-down, dead-battery support, PD message transmit and receive, and fast role swap. The digital part debounces Type-C level detection and interrupts, detects FRS, moves PD payload a byte at a time with DMA, divides the PD timing clock, generates and checks CRC, encodes and decodes 4b5b, handles ordered sets with a receive mask, and recovers frequency from the preamble. In Stop it can still detect incoming PD messages and FRS signalling.

CRS trims the internal 48 MHz oscillator automatically across the operating range from a sync source: USB SOF, the LSE, an external signal on CRS_SYNC or software. Manual trimming can be added to lock faster at start-up.

The flexible static memory controller (also called FMC) has a NOR/PSRAM controller and a NAND controller. It drives SRAM, NOR and OneNAND Flash, PSRAM (four banks), NAND Flash with hardware ECC over up to 8 Kbytes, and FRAM, on an 8- or 16-bit bus, with a chip select and configuration per bank and a write FIFO. Synchronous accesses run with FMC_CLK at up to HCLK/2. It also drives graphic LCD controllers in Intel 8080 or Motorola 6800 mode. It is present on the Vx, Px and Qx devices.

Interface for single, dual or quad SPI Flash in indirect mode (all through registers), status-polling mode (the Flash status register read periodically, with an interrupt on a flag) or memory-mapped mode (the Flash seen as internal memory). Dual-Flash mode drives two quad memories at once for twice the throughput and capacity. It supports SDR and DDR, a fully programmable opcode and frame, with instruction, address, alternate-byte, dummy and data phases each set for enable, length and line count; a receive/transmit FIFO; 8-, 16- and 32-bit accesses; DMA in indirect mode; flag masking; timeout handling; and interrupts on FIFO threshold, timeout, status match, completion and access error.

The SWJ-DP combines JTAG and serial-wire debug: SWD needs two pins, as SWDIO on JTMS and SWCLK on JTCK, and a sequence on TMS switches between JTAG-DP and SW-DP; unused JTAG pins can serve as GPIOs. The embedded trace macrocell streams compressed instruction and data trace through a few ETM pins (TRACECK, TRACED0 to TRACED3) to an external trace port analyser.

These three pins draw from the backup power switch, which sinks no more than 3 mA, so as outputs they are limited to 2 MHz into 30 pF and must not source current such as an LED's. After the backup domain powers up they are GPIOs governed by the RTC registers, which system reset does not clear.
PA13, PA14, PA15, PB3 and PB4 come out of reset as JTAG/SWD pins, with pull-ups on PA15, PA13 and PB4 and a pull-down on PA14.

PB6 (UCPD1_CC1) and PB4 (UCPD1_CC2) hold a 5.1 kΩ pull-down (Rd) inside the UCPD that can be on from reset: a high level on PA9 (UCPD1_DBCC1) turns on the one at PB6, and a high level on PA10 (UCPD1_DBCC2) the one at PB4. Setting UCPD1_DBDIS = 1 in PWR_CR3 removes them.

Voltages are referred to VSS. Min and max limits hold over the worst case of temperature, supply and clock, and are tested on every part at TA = 25 °C and at TA max of the temperature range. Limits marked as characterization, design or technology data are not tested; characterization limits are the mean ±3σ of a sample. Typical figures are at TA = 25 °C and VDD = VDDA = 3 V, as design guidance and untested. Typical ADC accuracy is the level 95 % of a batch from one diffusion lot meet over the full temperature range (mean ±2σ). Typical curves are design guidance and untested.

Every supply pair (VDD/VSS, VDDA/VSSA and so on) has filtering ceramic capacitors as in the power supply scheme: n x 100 nF plus one 4.7 µF on VDD, 10 nF plus 1 µF on VDDA and 100 nF plus 1 µF on VREF+. They go as close to the pins as possible, or under them on the bottom of the board.

Going past the voltage, current or thermal ratings can damage the part for good. They are stress limits only: operation there is not implied, and long exposure can reduce reliability. The mission profile meets JEDEC JESD47; longer profiles are available on request.

Supply current depends on the supply voltage, temperature, pin loads, software setup, clocks, pin toggling, where code runs and what it runs. The tables are taken with every I/O in analog input, every peripheral off unless named, Flash wait states at the minimum for fHCLK (RM0440), fPCLK = fHCLK when peripherals run, and Range 1 Boost for 150 MHz < fHCLK ≤ 170 MHz or Range 1 normal for 26 MHz < fHCLK ≤ 150 MHz.

An input with pull-up draws current, set by the pull-up value, whenever the pin is held low outside; output loads and pull-downs add their own. An input sitting at a mid-level voltage draws current through its Schmitt trigger: pins that need not be digital, the ADC, OPAMP and COMP inputs among them, are set to analog mode. A floating input can drift to mid-level or toggle with noise, so each one is put in analog mode or held at a level with a pull resistor or by making it an output.

Each peripheral figure is the difference in supply current between the peripheral clocked and not clocked, with every I/O in analog mode. It covers the digital part; the analog part of a peripheral is given with that peripheral.
Wakeup times run from the wakeup event to the first user instruction executed. The part enters the low-power mode on a WFE instruction.

In bypass the HSE or LSE oscillator is off and its input pin is an ordinary GPIO input: the external clock meets the I/O characteristics, and the timing diagram gives the recommended waveform (high and low times, 10 % and 90 % points).

HSE runs from a 4 MHz to 48 MHz crystal or ceramic resonator; its figures come from design simulation with typical external parts. The resonator and load capacitors sit as close to the oscillator pins as possible to keep distortion and start-up time down. CL1 and CL2 are high-quality ceramic capacitors for high frequency, typically 5 pF to 20 pF, usually equal, chosen so that their series value plus pin and board capacitance (about 10 pF to start) matches the crystal load capacitance. REXT depends on the crystal. AN2867 covers crystal choice.

LSE runs from a 32.768 kHz crystal; its figures come from design simulation with typical external parts. The crystal and load capacitors sit as close to the pins as possible. No resistor may be fitted between OSC32_IN and OSC32_OUT. LSEDRV[1:0] sets the drive from low to high, trading current against the largest crystal gm it can start.
HSI16, HSI48 and LSI figures are tested over the general operating conditions; their curves are characterization results and untested.

Susceptibility is sampled during characterization with the part toggling two LEDs. ESD is applied to every pin (IEC 61000-4-2) and fast transient bursts through 100 pF to VDD and VSS (IEC 61000-4-4) until the LEDs show a failure; a reset restores operation. Levels and classes follow AN1709. Results depend heavily on the application software, so the software handles runaway conditions (corrupted program counter, unexpected reset, corrupted control registers); forcing NRST or the oscillator pins low for 1 s reproduces most failures for prequalification (AN1015).
Emission is measured to IEC 61967-2, which fixes the test board and pin loading, with the part toggling two LEDs.

ESD: a positive then a negative pulse 1 s apart on each pin combination of 3 x (n + 1) samples, n being the number of supply pins (ANSI/JEDEC). Latch-up: three parts each take a supply overvoltage on every supply pin and current injection on every I/O pin (EIA/JESD 78E).

Voltages below VSS or above VDD on I/O pins are avoided in normal use. Robustness is sampled by injecting current into one floating input at a time while the part runs; a failure is an ADC error over 5 LSB TUE, induced leakage on neighbouring pins outside -5 µA/+0 µA, a reset or a clock shift. Negative injection causes negative induced leakage and positive injection positive.

All I/Os meet both CMOS and TTL levels with no setting. A GPIO sinks or sources up to ±8 mA, or ±20 mA with relaxed VOL/VOH. The current all I/Os source plus the part's own VDD current stays within ΣIVDD, and the current all I/Os sink plus the part's own VSS current within ΣIVSS.

OSPEEDRy[1:0] sets the output speed; Fm+ mode is set in SYSCFG_CFGR1. The maximum frequency holds when (tr + tf) ≤ 2/3 of the period and the duty cycle is 45 % to 55 % at the stated load. Speed 11 can toggle at up to 180 MHz into 10 pF, above the 170 MHz system clock.

NRST is a CMOS input with a permanent pull-up RPU (25 kΩ to 55 kΩ). Pulses under 70 ns are filtered and pulses over 350 ns reset the part. A 0.1 µF capacitor to ground close to the pin protects against parasitic resets; whatever drives NRST must bring it below VIL(NRST) max.

At fHRTIM = 170 MHz the step is 184 ps (TA -40 °C to 105 °C). The dead-time clock spans 0.125 to 16 tHRTIM and the dead time up to 511 tDTG (48.09 µs). Digital faults reach the outputs in 9 ns typ, comparator faults in 16 ns typ; low-latency external events 1 to 5 in 12 ns (digital) and 19 ns (analog), synchronous events 1 to 10 in 56 ns and 62 ns with 1 tHRTIM jitter.
An interrupt or event input pulse lasts at least 20 ns to be seen by the controller.

The analog switches of the I/Os have a voltage booster, on (BOOSTEN = 1 in SYSCFG_CFGR1) while VDDA < 2.4 V and off from 2.4 V. It starts in 240 µs max and draws up to 250 µA, 500 µA or 900 µA depending on VDD.

The ADC is calibrated after each power-up (116 ADC clocks, 1.93 µs at 60 MHz). It runs at up to 60 MHz alone in Range 1 (26 MHz in Range 2) and lower with all ADCs running. Fast channels are ADCx_IN1 to ADCx_IN5; the others are slow channels with a lower allowed RAIN. VREF+ may be tied to VDDA inside the package. Negative injection on one analog pin spoils conversions on others; a Schottky diode to ground on such pins prevents it. VDDA has a good ceramic capacitor close to the part, decoupled as in the power supply scheme.

Each DAC channel has an output buffer that lowers the output impedance to drive loads without an external op-amp; BOFFx in DAC_CR bypasses it. Buffered, the output needs RL ≥ 5 kΩ and CL ≤ 50 pF and can overshoot for low codes. Sample and hold mode keeps the output on CSH between refresh phases.

VREFBUF gives 2.048 V, 2.5 V or 2.9 V (VRS = 00, 01, 10) when VDDA is at least 2.4 V, 2.8 V or 3.135 V. Below that it is in degraded mode and its output follows VDDA less a drop. It needs 0.5 µF to 1.5 µF on its output, ESR ≤ 2 Ω, including a 100 nF low-ESR capacitor for high-frequency noise, and supplies up to 6.5 mA. Inrush at start-up and on a scale change is controlled while VDDA is inside the range of the chosen VRS.

The comparators run from 1.62 V, take inputs from 0 to VDDA, start in 5 µs and switch in 16.7 ns typ (VDDA ≥ 2.7 V, 50 pF load). Hysteresis is set by HYST[2:0] in eight steps from 0 to 63 mV typ. The scaler takes VREFINT as its input and draws 0.8 µA typ with its bridge on.

The op-amps run from 2 V to 3.6 V with a 0 to VDDA common-mode range, 13 MHz GBW and 6.5 V/µs (normal) or 45 V/µs (high-speed). As PGAs they give non-inverting gains of 2 to 64 and inverting gains of -1 to -63 with internal resistors; the PGA bandwidth is GBW divided by the non-inverting gain. With OPAINTOEN = 1 the output goes to the ADC internally, which needs a sampling time of 200 ns (VDDA ≥ 2 V) or 300 ns.
The sensor slopes 2.5 mV/°C typ and reads 0.76 V typ at 30 °C. The ADC result at 30 °C, measured at VDDA = 3.0 V ±10 mV, is stored in TS_CAL1. The ADC samples it for at least 5 µs.

VBAT is read through an internal 39 kΩ bridge that divides it by 3 (±10 %), sampled for at least 12 µs. A battery on VBAT can be charged through an internal 5 kΩ (VBRS = 0) or 1.5 kΩ (VBRS = 1) resistor.

Timer figures are guaranteed by design. At 170 MHz a timer resolves 5.88 ns, takes external clocks to 85 MHz and encoder inputs to 42.5 MHz; a 32-bit counter spans 25.26 s. IWDG timeouts at 32 kHz LSI run from 0.125 ms to 32768 ms with one LSI period of uncertainty from the clock phases; WWDG at 170 MHz PCLK runs from 0.0241 ms to 12.336 ms.

The I2C meets the I2C-bus specification rev. 03 timing for Standard-mode (100 kbit/s), Fast-mode (400 kbit/s) and Fast-mode Plus (1 Mbit/s) when configured per RM0440 with I2CCLK above the minimum for the mode. SDA and SCL are not true open-drain: the PMOS to the I/O supply is off but present. The 20 mA Fm+ sink is met only in part, which caps the Fm+ bus load. Every SDA and SCL pin has an analog spike filter of 50 ns to 90 ns.

SPI and FMC timings are taken with OSPEEDRy[1:0] = 11 and 30 pF; I2S, SAI and USART with OSPEEDRy[1:0] = 10 and 30 pF; Quad SPI with 11 and 15 pF or 20 pF. All are measured at 0.5 x VDD. The SAI needs an APB clock at least twice its own clock.
FDCANx_TX and FDCANx_RX follow the I/O port characteristics.

The USB device is USB 2.0 full-speed compliant and USB-IF certified. It works without a crystal from -15 °C to 85 °C. It works down to 2.7 V, with degraded electrical figures between 2.7 V and 3.0 V. The DP pull-up and the driver matching impedance are inside, so no series resistors go on D+ and D-.

Asynchronous timings use AddressSetupTime, AddressHoldTime, DataHoldTime, ByteLaneSetup and DataSetupTime = 0x1 (DataSetupTime = 0x5 in NWAIT mode) and BusTurnAroundDuration = 0x0. Synchronous timings use burst access enabled, CRAM memory type, write burst enabled, CLKDivision = 1 and DataLatency = 1 for NOR or 0 for PSRAM. NAND timings use COM and ATT setup 0x01, wait 0x03, hold 0x02, HiZ 0x01, a 16-bit NAND bank with ECC on over 512-byte pages, and TCLRSetupTime = TARSetupTime = 0. THCLK is the HCLK period throughout.
UCPD1 complies with the Type-C specification (rev. 1.2) and with Power Delivery rev. 3.0. It needs VDD of 3.0 V to 3.6 V as a sink only, and 3.135 V to 3.465 V as sink and source.

Nine packages: WLCSP81 (4.02 x 4.27 mm, 0.4 mm ball pitch), UFQFPN48 (7 x 7 mm, 0.5 mm pitch, exposed pad), LQFP48 (7 x 7 mm), LQFP64 (10 x 10 mm), LQFP80 (12 x 12 mm), TFBGA100 (8 x 8 mm, 0.8 mm ball pitch), LQFP100 (14 x 14 mm), LQFP128 (14 x 14 mm, 0.4 mm pitch) and UFBGA121 (6 x 6 mm, 0.5 mm ball pitch). All are ECOPACK grades.

The top side carries the product identification on two lines, a date code (year and week), a revision code and a pin 1 or ball A1 mark; the markings vary with the supply chain, and further supply-chain marks may be present. Parts marked ES or E, or shipped with an engineering-sample notice, are not qualified for production.

Each temperature suffix guarantees an ambient temperature at full dissipation and a maximum junction temperature (6: 85 °C ambient, 105 °C junction; 3: 125 °C ambient, 130 °C junction). Few designs run at full dissipation, so the real dissipation and junction temperature decide the suffix. Example at high performance: TAmax 82 °C, IDDmax 50 mA at VDD 3.5 V, 20 outputs low at 8 mA and 0.4 V plus 8 outputs low at 20 mA and 1.3 V give PINTmax 175 mW, PI/Omax 272 mW and PDmax 447 mW; in LQFP100 at 42 °C/W, TJmax = 82 °C + 18.774 °C = 100.774 °C, inside suffix 6 (TJ below 105 °C). At that dissipation suffix 6 allows TAmax 86.226 °C and suffix 3 allows 111.226 °C.

TAmax 100 °C, IDDmax 20 mA at VDD 3.5 V and 20 outputs low at 8 mA and 0.4 V give PINTmax 70 mW, PI/Omax 64 mW and PDmax 134 mW. In LQFP100 at 42 °C/W, TJmax = 100 °C + 5.628 °C = 105.628 °C, above the suffix 6 limit of 105 °C: suffix 3 is needed unless the dissipation is lowered.
